items.title: Edison lost the war of currents in the 1890s
items.claim: Thomas Edison championed direct current (DC) for distributing electricity. George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla pushed alternating current (AC). By 1895 AC had won — and every domestic supply on Earth is now AC for a single decisive technical reason.
items.prompt: Why did AC beat DC for power distribution?

options.text: AC can be stepped up to very high voltage (low current) for long-distance transmission and stepped back down for domestic use using transformers — DC cannot easily be transformed, so it loses huge amounts of energy as heat in distribution cables
DC produces more harmful magnetic fields

items.reveal_title: Power dissipation scales as I squared R
items.reveal:
Power loss in a transmission line is I squared times R. For a given power delivered (P = VI), higher voltage means lower current, and so vastly lower losses. Transformers (Faraday's induction, 1831) require an alternating magnetic flux — AC works, DC does not.

UK grid runs at 50 Hz; US, Mexico, parts of Brazil run at 60 Hz. The choice was historical (early generators in Europe vs America had different design constants) and is now too embedded to change.

High-voltage DC transmission HAS become possible since the 1950s (solid-state converters) and is now used for very long undersea cables. But local distribution to homes is still AC because that's what every appliance and wall socket has been built around.
items.why: AC's dominance is taught as a historical fact. The deeper reason is the I squared R loss in transmission combined with transformers' need for changing flux.

items.title: In space no one can hear you scream — sound needs a medium
items.claim: Sound is a pressure wave that propagates by compressing and rarefying particles of a medium. In a vacuum, there are no particles. Light travels through vacuum fine; sound cannot.
items.prompt: Why doesn't sound propagate in vacuum?

options.text: Sound is a mechanical wave — successive layers of atoms or molecules push on their neighbours. Without matter, there is no medium to compress and rarefy

items.reveal:
Sound is a longitudinal wave: layers of medium are compressed and rarefied in the direction of propagation. The wave needs a medium with mass (to carry inertia) and stiffness (to provide restoring force).

Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) are different: they are self-supporting oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and need no medium. They cross interstellar vacuum easily.

Robert Boyle (1660) demonstrated this experimentally: he placed a ringing bell inside a glass jar and pumped out the air. As the air thinned, the bell sound faded. With a near-vacuum, no sound got out — but he could still see the clapper striking. The mechanical wave needed air; the light didn't.
items.why: Sound and light are both 'waves' — but require entirely different conditions to propagate. The vacuum distinguishes them sharply.

items.title: An electron interferes with itself
items.claim: Fire electrons one at a time at a screen with two slits. With BOTH slits open, the pattern that builds up is the classic interference fringe — even though only one electron is in flight at any moment.
items.prompt: What gets in the way of saying 'each electron goes through one slit or the other'?

options.text: Nothing — each electron does go through one slit

If you measure which slit each electron uses, the interference pattern disappears — the electron behaves as a particle. Without the measurement, the wavefunction passes through both slits and self-interferes
Multiple electrons collide in flight and create the pattern
The fringe pattern is an artefact of the screen, not the electrons

items.reveal:
Before measurement, the electron's wavefunction is a superposition of 'through slit 1' and 'through slit 2' paths. The interference fringes are the result of these amplitudes adding and cancelling at the detector.

Add any apparatus capable of detecting which slit the electron went through — even in principle — and the interference vanishes. The state has become entangled with the detector and no longer interferes with itself.

This is the heart of quantum mechanics. It's not about ignorance. It's not 'we don't know which slit'. It's that, until measured, the electron is in BOTH paths in a coherent superposition that has measurable effects (the fringes).
items.why: Particles have definite positions in classical physics. Quantum particles don't — their position is a probability distribution that depends on what you can in principle know.
